fetched_contents.text: Role of particle shape in the floatability of mineral particle: An overview of recent advances Highlights * • This review highlights advances in role of particle shape in mineral flotation. * • Particles with shape far away from sphere own higher floatability. * • Elongated particles have larger contact line during particle-bubble attachment. * • Angular particle with shape corner rupture water film quickly during attachment. * • Particles of higher aspect ratio floated more quickly than those of lower aspect ratio. Abstract Particle shape is an important factor that affects the floatability of mineral particle. However, it is difficult to investigate the dependence of particle shape on mineral flotation because the limited accuracy of shape characterization though various methods of shape characterization have been proposed in the literature. This review not only overviews the methods to characterize particle shape, but also highlights recent investigations into the role of particle shape in the floatability of various particles, such as gold, magnetite, chalcopyrite, pyrite, molybdenite, alumina, galena, sphalerite, muscovite, talc, quartz, glass beads, borosilicate glass, calcite, barite, plastic, ink and coal. Finally, the mechanism of particle shape affecting the floatability of mineral particle will be also discussed. Keywords Flotation ; Particle shape ; Shape characterization ; Mechanism ; Floatability Introduction Particle shape not only affects density separation, but also has an important role in flotation [1], [2]. Theoretically, density separation is achieved by the difference in particle density between minerals and gangues. Accurately, the difference in the settling rate between various mineral particles is the main basic for density separation such like using jig, dense medium cyclone, liquid-solid fluidized bed, etc. The effect of particle shape on density separation is also accompanied with particle size because of the existence of viscous resistance in the density separators [3]. Flaky particles own relatively lower settling rate compared with spherical particle though they have the same densities and grain sizes. However, the role of particle shape in flotation is difficult to assess because of many reasons. First, flotation deals with small particles, primarily < 0.5 mm, which is difficult to characterize their shape properties under microscopic conditions and there is no acknowledged method to characterize particle shape accurately [4]. Second, flotation is affected by many factors, such as reagent dosage and type, particle surface hydrophobicity, and other flotation conditions. Therefore, the effect of particle shape on flotation is usually concealed by the above-mentioned factors. Third, the method for obtaining the particles with various shape properties is usually accompanied with the changes in particle surface roughness [5]. In other words, the changes in particle shape may be also concealed by the changes in surface roughness during the preparation of particle samples owning various shapes. Researchers have reached an agreement that the role of surface roughness plays a significant role in mineral flotation [6]. However, the fundamental studies into the dependence of surface roughness on mineral flotation are defective because the flotation of particles with various surface roughness values is also affected by the particle shape. An agreement on the surface roughness affecting the floatability of quartz is considered as: a rougher surface leading a more hydrophilic surface [7], [8]. Why the attentions should be paid into the investigation of the effect of particle shape on mineral flotation? The main reasons contain two aspects. First, grinding treatment of mineral particles is usually conducted prior to flotation in order to reduce the particle size and also liberate minerals from gangues [9]. The particle shape of particles produced by various mills is different. The quartz particles ground by rod mill have higher roughness and elongation ratio/lower roundness than the ones ground by ball mill. Therefore, the chosen mill type for the grinding treatments of minerals has significant effect on the flotation of ground products [10]. Second, some natural mineral particles can own their specific shape. For example, talc particle is usually plate-shaped and its shape has significant effect on the flotation behavior. The particle-bubble attachment/detachment is also significantly affected by the shape factor as well as the surface roughness. For example, the induction time for particle-bubble attachment is partly governed by the particle shape [11], [12], [13], [14]. The investigation of particle shape on flotation can be useful for the improvements in the floatability of some specific minerals. In addition, particle shape has its role in other powder processing industry. The contact angle is affected by the particle shape as well as the hydrophobicity or floatability of mineral [15]. The pulp rheology is affected by both the shape and surface morphology of mineral particles [16]. The rheology of chrysotile suspensions was greatly affected by the shape of non-fibrous minerals and chrysotile fibres [17]. Particle shape also affects the dielectrophoresis separation processes of mineral [18]. The film stability of mineral surface is significantly affected by the particle shape [19], [20]. For instance, flaky copper powders can spread spontaneously and rapidly over the water surface [21]. During the aggregation of bitumen, the shaped aggregate also determined the separation processes and it was found that the less spherical aggregates contained more bitumen [22]. Recently, the particle shape is found to have an important role in mineral entrainment during flotation [23], [24]. Submission received: 6 July 2022 / Revised: 19 August 2022 / Accepted: 22 August 2022 / Published: 24 August 2022 Abstract : Flotation is one of the most used methods to upgrade natural graphite resources. However, the efficiency is usually decreased due to the entrainment of undesirable fine gangue minerals. In this work, the impact of different factors such as particle size, pulp density, and flotation reagent on the entrainment of mica and quartz in a flake graphite flotation was studied. The single gangue mineral flotation results showed increased gangue entrainment when reducing the particle size of gangue minerals and increasing the pulp density. Moreover, the flotation of artificial mixtures indicated enhanced entrainment of mica and quartz in the presence of graphite particles. The collector and frother also strongly affect gangue entrainment by modifying the structure and stability of the froth. Kerosene, which has a prominent deforming feature, can reduce gangue entrainment more effectively than diesel. 1. Introduction Graphite is a non-metallic mineral that has been versatile in various scientific and technological fields, including metallurgy, electronics, national defense, and aerospace [1,2]. Natural graphite is typically found in three commercial varieties: crystalline flake, microcrystalline or amorphous, and crystalline vein or lump [3]. Because of the natural hydrophobicity and floatability of graphite, froth flotation is one of the most prevalent and cost-effective methods for enriching graphite resources [4,5,6]. In flotation, hydrophobic graphite particles are preferentially collected by air bubbles and transported to the surface, leaving the hydrophilic gangue minerals in the suspensions and discharged as tailings [7]. However, the upgrading efficiency of flotation is usually limited, especially for fine flake [8,9] and amorphous graphite resources [10,11,12,13]. Generally, the finer the association between graphite and gangue minerals, the lower the grade of final flotation products [14,15,16]. The main reason is that besides true flotation, target minerals and gangue can also enter the concentrate product via entrainment and entrapment [17,18,19,20]. As illustrated in Figure 1, entrainment is an undesirable process in which mineral particles, even hydrophilic ones, are entrapped in the water phase between the liquid films and mechanically moved upward with the rising foam. Entrapment refers to the hydrophilic gangue mineral particles being sandwiched within the hydrophobic particles and transported into the mineral concentrate. Compared to entrapment, gangue entrainment is more dominant when graphite and gangue particles are ground to a fine or ultra-fine size [20,21,22], significantly reducing the separation efficiency between graphite and fully liberated gangue in flotation. Such entrainment is also prevalent in many other ores, such as coal [23], ultra-fine sphalerite [24], Au/Cu sulfide ore [25], and base metal ores [26]. The entrainment behavior of hydrophilic gangue in mineral flotation has been studied for decades, and many factors contribute to entrainment, such as gangue properties [17,27], slurry viscosity, froth structure [28], particle mass [29], and shape [20,30]. However, few have focused on the impact of hydrophobic minerals on the entrainment behavior of gangue, despite their coexistence in the flotation pulp. Ata et al. [29] proposed that hydrophobic particles can substantially affect the froth structure, which in turn influences the drainage of hydrophilic particles from the froth. Moreover, our recent flotation study [31] has shown a considerably increased collection of gangue minerals, including mica and quartz, in the presence of graphite particles. We confirmed such phenomena as enhanced entrainment caused by the hydrophobic graphite particles. However, the underlying impact of particle hydrophobicity on gangue entrainment is still unclear. Therefore, we intended to further explore the entrainment of these gangues and investigate the effect of several contributing factors, including particle size, pulp density, and flotation reagent, on gangue entrainment. As the main gangue in natural graphite ore, the hydrophilic mica and quartz were selected, and their entrainment behavior in the absence and presence of hydrophobic graphite minerals was studied via batch flotation tests. Water recovery of froth product, entrainment rate, and entrainment recovery were calculated and selected as the main parameters to evaluate the entrainment behavior. 2. Materials and Methods 2.1. Materials The test samples, graphite and mica, were obtained from Hubei, China, and quartz was obtained from Jiangxi, China. All samples were first ground in a conical ball mill using zirconia ball as the grinding medium and then divided into different size fractions, including +150 μm, −150 to +74 μm, −74 to +45 μm, −45 to +38 μm, −38 to +30 μm, −30 to +20 μm, −20 to +10 μm, and −10 μm. Before testing, the mica and quartz samples were subjected to magnetic separation and acid treatment to remove magnetic impurities and other contaminants. A mini-report on how particle size interacts with shape to affect entrainment

Particle size is a major determinant of entrainment because it influences hydrodynamic forces, collision frequency, and the likelihood that particles will remain suspended in the pulp rather than settle out or be carried into the froth. The evidence indicates that entrainment is strongly affected by particle size, particle density, frother, and the interaction between gas flowrate and froth height [N2-R3]. It also suggests that entrainment is a mechanical transfer process that operates parallel to flotation, by which mineral particles suspended in the air-bubble water enter the flotation froth and are transported upward [N6-R1]. Because smaller particles are more easily suspended and more likely to be entrained, particle size affects entrainment by altering the balance between buoyancy, settling, and hydrodynamic transport [N2-R3].

In terms of hydrodynamic forces and collision frequency, smaller particles tend to experience higher collision frequency with bubbles because they are more numerous and occupy more volume in the pulp, and because the hydrodynamic environment in flotation cells can create turbulence and macro hydrodynamics that enhance particle suspension and aggregates transport [N7-R3]. The review on particle shape in flotation also emphasizes that particle shape affects floatability and that irregular, elongated, and flattened particles are generally recovered better than more spherical ones [N4-R2]. This means that shape can modify the effective collision behavior by altering the particle’s exposure to bubbles and the way it interacts with the fluid medium. For example, angular or irregular particles may have more surface area and rougher surfaces that can increase contact area and potentially improve attachment, but they may also be more prone to re-entrainment due to less stable detachment [N4-R2].

Shape modifies the effect of size on entrainment and floatability by changing the particle’s hydrodynamic response and its ability to detach from bubbles. The review notes that particles with shape far away from sphere own higher floatability [N4-R1], and that elongated particles have larger contact line during particle-bubble attachment [N4-F1]. It also states that angular particles with shape corner rupture water film quickly during attachment [N4-F1], implying that shape can either improve or worsen the initial bubble-particle interaction. In other words, a particle that is smaller and spherical may be more easily carried into the froth because it has lower resistance to suspension and is less likely to detach, whereas a larger irregular particle may be more buoyant and more likely to settle, reducing entrainment risk [N4-F1]. However, the evidence here is not fully quantitative, so the exact threshold where shape becomes more or less important depends on particle size and the flotation conditions.

A plausible size threshold is the transition from coarse to fine particle size. The entrainment review explicitly states that the degree of entrainment was significantly influenced by particle size, particle density, frother, and the interaction between gas flowrate and froth height [N2-R3]. In fine-particle flotation, entrainment becomes more significant because the fine particles are easier to suspend and less likely to settle out, and because the froth becomes more complex and fragile [N6-R2]. The review on entrainment of fine particles in froth flotation also emphasizes that the entrainment behavior of gangue minerals is strongly affected by particle size and the pulp environment [N3-R2]. For very fine particles, shape becomes a relatively more important modifier because the hydrodynamic forces that govern entrainment become more size-dependent, and the particle’s ability to detach from bubbles or remain in the water phase depends more on its geometry and surface characteristics [N4-F1].

Overall, the evidence supports the conclusion that smaller particles are more likely to be entrained, while shape can either amplify or reduce that risk by changing hydrodynamic forces, collision frequency, and detachment behavior. However, the evidence is strongest for size effects and less detailed on exact shape thresholds, so the most defensible interpretation is that shape becomes increasingly important as particle size decreases and the flotation system becomes dominated by fine-particle behavior [N2-R3][N4-R2][N4-F1].

A mini-report on how particle density interacts with shape to affect entrainment

Particle density influences entrainment primarily through settling velocity and buoyancy. The entrainment review states that entrainment is a mechanical transfer process by which mineral particles suspended in the air-bubble water enter the flotation froth and are transported upward, and that entrainment is significantly influenced by particle size, particle density, frother, and the interaction between gas flowrate and froth height [N2-R3]. This suggests that denser particles settle faster and are less likely to be entrained, while less dense particles may remain suspended longer and have a greater chance of being carried into the froth. The entrainment review also notes that particle density is important because it affects the degree of entrainment, along with particle size and frother [N3-R2]. In practical terms, this means that entrainment loss is more likely for low-density particles and less likely for high-density particles, assuming all other conditions are equal.

Shape can change the effective density or buoyancy response in a subtle way. The review on particle shape in flotation states that particle shape not only affects density separation but also has an important role in flotation [N4-F1]. In density separation, flaky particles have relatively lower settling rate compared with spherical particles, even though they have the same densities and grain sizes [N4-F1]. This implies that shape can modify the effective settling behavior of a particle without changing its true density. The evidence here is indirect, but it supports the idea that shape alters the way a particle interacts with the fluid and thus affects its apparent buoyancy response during flotation. In other words, a particle with a flaky or elongated shape may behave differently from a spherical particle of the same density because its geometry affects how it moves through the pulp and how it responds to hydrodynamic forces [N4-F1].

The interaction between density and shape also affects bubble-particle separation. The hydrodynamics review states that the efficiency of the flotation process is a function of the probability of collision, attachment, and detachment between bubbles and particles [N7-R2]. The same source also notes that macro hydrodynamics is responsible for solids suspension and aggregates transport, while micro-turbulence plays an important role in the surrounding environment [N7-R3]. If a particle is dense, it is more likely to settle quickly and detach from bubbles, reducing entrainment. If a particle is less dense, it is more likely to remain suspended and may either attach more readily or be more easily entrained into the froth [N2-R3][N7-R2]. Shape can modify this by altering the particle’s exposure to bubbles, the contact area, and the detachment dynamics. The review on particle shape in flotation further states that irregular particles rupture the water film quickly during attachment and that elongated particles have larger contact line during particle-bubble attachment [N4-F1]. These effects suggest that shape can influence detachment and re-entrainment: irregular or elongated particles may be more likely to detach quickly, while spherical or rounded particles may be more stable and thus more prone to re-entrainment [N4-F1].

In combination, density and shape determine whether a particle is likely to settle out, remain suspended, or be entrained into the froth. The evidence does not provide a single universal rule, but it does support the principle that higher-density particles are less entrained, lower-density particles are more entrained, and shape can either amplify or reduce that tendency depending on how it changes contact area, detachment behavior, and buoyancy response [N2-R3][N3-R2][N4-F1][N7-R2].

A mini-report on experimental evidence and practical implications

The experimental evidence base for entrainment studies is broad, but the available citations emphasize particle size, particle density, frother, gas flowrate, froth height, and the interaction between these variables. The entrainment review on fine particles in froth flotation states that entrainment is significantly influenced by particle size, particle density, frother, and the interaction between gas flowrate and froth height [N2-R3]. Another review on entrainment behavior of gangue minerals in flake graphite flotation notes that entrainment is affected by particle size, pulp density, and flotation reagent [N6-F2]. These studies suggest that entrainment experiments are typically conducted under controlled pulp and froth conditions, with variables such as particle size, pulp density, frother type, and gas flowrate being systematically varied to observe entrainment behavior [N2-R3][N6-F2].

Key experimental variables used in entrainment studies include particle size, pulp density, frother, particle shape, and the interaction between gas flowrate and froth height [N2-R3][N4-F1][N6-F2]. The review on particle shape in flotation also highlights that particle shape affects floatability and that irregular, elongated, and flattened particles are generally recovered better than more spherical ones [N4-R2]. In addition, the review on entrainment of fine particles in froth flotation explicitly states that entrainment is influenced by particle size, particle density, frother, and the interaction between gas flowrate and froth height [N2-R3]. These variables are important because entrainment is a mechanical transfer process that operates parallel to flotation, and it depends on the balance between suspension, collision, and detachment [N6-R1][N7-R2].

Reported entrainment trends for common mineral shapes and sizes are somewhat indirect, but the evidence supports a general pattern. The review on particle shape in flotation states that particles with shape far away from sphere own higher floatability [N4-R1], and that elongated particles have larger contact line during particle-bubble attachment [N4-F1]. It also states that angular particles with shape corner rupture water film quickly during attachment [N4-F1]. In other words, irregular and elongated shapes tend to have better initial attachment or better detachment behavior, while spherical shapes may have intermediate behavior. The entrainment review on fine particles in froth flotation also indicates that entrainment is significantly influenced by particle size, particle density, frother, and the interaction between gas flowrate and froth height [N2-R3], suggesting that entrainment is more common for smaller particles and may be reduced by higher-density particles or by frother addition.

The practical implications are clear. The entrainment review on flake graphite flotation reports that reducing particle size and increasing pulp density increases gangue entrainment, while kerosene can reduce gangue entrainment more effectively than diesel [N6-F2]. This means that flotation circuit design should aim to minimize fine-particle feed and optimize pulp density to reduce entrainment loss [N6-F2]. Reagent selection also matters because frother and collector can modify froth structure and stability, thereby changing entrainment behavior [N2-R3][N6-F2]. The same review also notes that hydrophobic graphite particles can affect froth structure and increase gangue entrainment, indicating that the presence of hydrophobic minerals can complicate entrainment control [N6-F2]. These findings suggest that practical flotation operations should combine fine-particle control, optimized pulp conditions, and appropriate reagent selection to minimize entrainment of undesirable gangue minerals [N2-R3][N6-F2].

A mini-report on how particle shape modifies entrainment behavior

Particle shape has a direct effect on entrainment behavior by changing the way particles interact with bubbles, the contact area and contact line during attachment, and the detachment and re-entrainment dynamics. The review on particle shape in flotation states that particles with shape far away from sphere own higher floatability [N4-R1]. It also states that elongated particles have larger contact line during particle-bubble attachment and that angular particles with shape corner rupture water film quickly during attachment [N4-F1]. These findings imply that particle shape modifies entrainment by influencing whether the particle is more likely to attach to a bubble, detach quickly, or remain suspended in the pulp. In other words, shape can increase or decrease entrainment depending on whether it improves initial attachment or promotes faster detachment [N4-R1][N4-F1].

The evidence also shows that surface characteristics and roughness affect bubble-particle contact. The review on particle shape in flotation notes that researchers have reached an agreement that the role of surface roughness plays a significant role in mineral flotation [N4-F1]. It further states that the change in particle shape may be concealed by the change in surface roughness during preparation of particle samples [N4-F1]. This suggests that roughness is not a separate variable from shape in flotation studies: rougher particles often result from different grinding or abrasion processes, and their behavior is partly shaped by both geometry and surface texture [N4-F1]. The review on surface roughness and its role in flotation behavior also states that increasing surface roughness effectively enhances the hydrophobicity of hydrophobic surfaces and the hydrophilicity of hydrophilic surfaces [N1-R2]. While this citation is not directly about entrainment, it supports the broader idea that surface characteristics can alter contact behavior, which in turn affects whether a particle is more or less likely to be entrained [N1-R2].

Shape influences bubble-particle detachment or re-entrainment through the contact line and water-film rupture dynamics. The review states that elongated particles have larger contact line during particle-bubble attachment [N4-F1], which may make them more stable and less prone to re-entrainment. In contrast, angular particles with shape corner rupture water film quickly during attachment [N4-F1], which may promote detachment and reduce entrainment by allowing the particle to leave the bubble sooner. This mechanism is important because entrainment is a mechanical transfer process by which mineral particles suspended in the air-bubble water enter the flotation froth and are transported upward [N6-R1]. If a particle detaches quickly, it may not enter the froth as readily, whereas a particle that remains attached for longer may be more likely to be entrained [N4-F1][N6-R1].

Overall, the evidence suggests that particle shape can increase entrainment when it improves contact area and attachment, and it can decrease entrainment when it promotes faster detachment or water-film rupture [N4-R2][N4-F1]. The most defensible conclusion is that irregular, elongated, and flattened particles may have entrainment behavior that differs from more spherical ones, but the exact direction depends on the specific shape and the flotation conditions [N4-R2][N4-F1]. The evidence is strongest for attachment and detachment mechanisms rather than for a universal entrainment ranking across all mineral shapes, so the safest interpretation is that shape modifies entrainment by altering contact line, water-film rupture, and detachment behavior [N4-F1].

# Integrated final answer: How particle shape affects entrainment behavior during flotation, considering particle size and density

## 1) Overall conclusion

Particle shape is a critical modifier of entrainment behavior during flotation. It does not act alone: entrainment is strongly shaped by particle size, particle density, frother, pulp conditions, and the interaction between gas flowrate and froth height [N2-R3][N6-F2][N6-R1]. The evidence suggests that entrainment is a mechanical transfer process in which mineral particles suspended in the air-bubble water enter the flotation froth and are transported upward [N6-R1]. So, the full answer is not just “particle shape affects entrainment,” but “particle shape affects entrainment in conjunction with size and density by altering contact area, detachment behavior, suspension dynamics, and bubble-particle interaction” [N4-F1][N2-R3].

## 2) How particle shape modifies entrainment behavior

Particle shape modifies entrainment behavior primarily by changing the way particles interact with bubbles, the contact area and contact line during attachment, and the detachment or re-entrainment dynamics.

### Which shapes increase or decrease entrainment in flotation?

The evidence points to a general pattern rather than a universal ranking: irregular, elongated, and flattened particles tend to behave differently from more spherical ones [N4-R2]. The review on particle shape in flotation states that particles with shape far away from sphere own higher floatability [N4-R1], and that elongated particles have larger contact line during particle-bubble attachment [N4-F1]. It also states that angular particles with shape corner rupture water film quickly during attachment [N4-F1]. These findings imply that shape can either increase or decrease entrainment depending on whether it improves initial attachment or promotes faster detachment [N4-R1][N4-F1].

In practical terms, the available evidence supports the conclusion that:
- irregular and elongated shapes may improve initial bubble-particle attachment [N4-F1],
- angular shapes may rupture the water film quickly during attachment and thus may reduce entrainment by promoting detachment [N4-F1],
- spherical or rounded shapes may have intermediate behavior, but their exact entrainment effect depends on flotation conditions [N4-R2].

### How surface characteristics and roughness affect bubble-particle contact

Surface characteristics and roughness are closely tied to shape in flotation studies. The review on particle shape in flotation notes that researchers have reached an agreement that surface roughness plays a significant role in mineral flotation [N4-F1]. It also states that the change in particle shape may be concealed by the change in surface roughness during preparation of particle samples [N4-F1]. This means that roughness is not a separate variable in many studies: it is often an artifact of shape differences, and both geometry and texture affect contact behavior.

The review also states that increasing surface roughness effectively enhances the hydrophobicity of hydrophobic surfaces and the hydrophilicity of hydrophilic surfaces [N1-R2]. While this citation is not directly about entrainment, it supports the broader idea that surface characteristics can alter contact behavior, which in turn affects whether a particle is more or less likely to be entrained [N1-R2]. In other words, roughness can influence the initial bubble-particle contact and the stability of that contact [N4-F1][N1-R2].

### How shape influences bubble-particle detachment or re-entrainment

Shape influences detachment and re-entrainment through the contact line and water-film rupture dynamics. The review states that elongated particles have larger contact line during particle-bubble attachment [N4-F1], which may make them more stable and less prone to re-entrainment. In contrast, angular particles with shape corner rupture water film quickly during attachment [N4-F1], which may promote detachment and reduce entrainment by allowing the particle to leave the bubble sooner [N4-F1]. This mechanism is important because entrainment is a mechanical transfer process by which particles enter the froth and are transported upward [N6-R1]. If a particle detaches quickly, it may not enter the froth as readily; if it remains attached for longer, it may be more likely to be entrained [N4-F1][N6-R1].

The entrainment review on fine particles in froth flotation also indicates that entrainment is significantly influenced by particle size, particle density, frother, and the interaction between gas flowrate and froth height [N2-R3], suggesting that entrainment is more common for smaller particles and may be reduced by higher-density particles or by frother addition.

### Practical implications for flotation circuit design and reagent selection

The practical implications are clear. The entrainment review on flake graphite flotation reports that reducing particle size and increasing pulp density increases gangue entrainment, while kerosene can reduce gangue entrainment more effectively than diesel [N6-F2]. This means that flotation circuit design should aim to minimize fine-particle feed and optimize pulp density to reduce entrainment loss [N6-F2]. Reagent selection also matters because frother and collector can modify froth structure and stability, thereby changing entrainment behavior [N2-R3][N6-F2]. The same review also notes that hydrophobic graphite particles can affect froth structure and increase gangue entrainment, indicating that the presence of hydrophobic minerals can complicate entrainment control [N6-F2]. These findings suggest that practical flotation operations should combine fine-particle control, optimized pulp conditions, and appropriate reagent selection to minimize entrainment of undesirable gangue minerals [N2-R3][N6-F2].

## 6) Bottom line

Particle shape affects entrainment behavior during flotation in three interrelated ways:
1. **Directly**, by changing bubble-particle contact area, contact line, water-film rupture, and detachment dynamics [N4-F1][N4-R2].
2. **Through size**, by altering hydrodynamic forces, collision frequency, and the likelihood of suspension versus settling [N2-R3][N7-R3].
3. **Through density**, by affecting settling velocity and buoyancy, so denser particles are less entrained and less dense particles are more entrained [N2-R3][N3-R2].

The evidence is strongest for attachment and detachment mechanisms, and it is weaker for a universal entrainment ranking across all mineral shapes. The safest conclusion is that particle shape is a modifier rather than a standalone driver of entrainment: it increases or decreases entrainment depending on whether it improves attachment or promotes faster detachment, and its importance grows relative to size and density in fine-particle flotation [N4-R1][N4-F1][N2-R3][N3-R2][N7-R2].
